entries.title: South Korea pledges legal action over alleged fuel exports to Russia
entries.summary: Ukrainian reports of South Korean fuel exports to Russia come amid strained tensions between Seoul and Kyiv.
entries.content:
Ukrainian reports of South Korean fuel exports to Russia come amid strained tensions between Seoul and Kyiv.

South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said the government will take legal action over illegal fuel shipments to Russia if allegations from an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are confirmed.

The Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had not confirmed whether South Korean fuel, including diesel, had been exported to Russia.

It added that exports of some products, such as diesel and jet fuel for commercial purposes, were not included in a South Korean exports control list to Russia.

On Wednesday, the South Korean presidential office dismissed a statement by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on sanctions policy, that 176,000 tonnes of fuel were shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers in July and August.

Ukraine’s top sanctions official said the alleged findings run counter to South Korea’s sanctions policy towards Russia.

“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, our government has consistently implemented sanctions and export controls against Russia in close cooperation with the international community,” South Korean presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said on Wednesday, according to the Yonhap news agency.

“We ask that Ukraine also refrain from distorting the relevant policies of the Republic of Korea without sufficient verification of the facts and making public remarks that can damage international trust,” she added.

Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been strained for the past couple of weeks after Seoul accused Zelenskyy of having “unilaterally disclosed” to the United Nations General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

Seoul Korea demanded an official apology from Kyiv, claiming the Ukrainian president had breached a non-disclosure agreement. Kyiv said no such agreement was in place.

Pyongyang and Moscow, meanwhile, have deep ties, with the two countries having signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024. According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts against Ukraine.

North Korea and South Korea remain technically at war because the 1950–1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

entries.title: US bars Fiji-based man over corruption tied to China
entries.summary: The State Department has accused the man of paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance Chinese interests.
entries.content:
The State Department has accused the official of paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance Chinese interests.

The US Department of State has publicly designated a Fiji-based man for his involvement in corruption on behalf of Chinese actors.

Zhao Fugang, the director of the Overseas Chinese Service Center, “abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business, and criminal interests”, the State Department said in a press release on Wednesday.

“His actions constituted significant corruption and adversely affected U.S. interests in Fiji.”

The designation renders Zhao and his immediate family members “generally ineligible for entry into the United States”.

The US embassy in Suva, Fiji’s capital, said Zhao’s actions left the Pacific nation open to “malign foreign influence facilitated by Chinese government, business, and criminal actors”.

The embassy also said, “Public reporting shows an established trend of criminals operating across the Pacific with ties to China.”

Beijing says Overseas Chinese Service Centers help its nationals with administrative issues abroad, such as renewing driving licences. However, rights groups have alleged they are fronts for Beijing to push interests abroad, including the targeting of dissidents.

In February, the Trump administration sanctioned two leaders of Pacific island nations for alleged corruption tied to China. The US Department of State issued a notice alleging that Hokkons Baules, the president of Palau’s Senate, and Anderson Jibas, a former mayor in the Marshall Islands, had created openings for China to increase its influence in the region.

entries.title: Tanker hit by multiple projectiles off north coast of Qatar, UKMTO says
entries.summary: The UK maritime agency has reported a rise in attacks on vessels in the vital Strait of Hormuz.
entries.content:
British maritime agency has recently reported a rise in attacks on vessels in the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz.

A number of casualties have been reported after a tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar was struck by multiple projectiles, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency has announced.

The vessel was hit by several projectiles 94 kilometres (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, UKMTO said on Wednesday. The incident comes as the British maritime agency reported a recent rise in attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

UKMTO did not say how many people were killed or injured in this latest attack, adding that authorities were investigating. It did not specify the origin of the ship.

An attack on a vessel in the middle of the Gulf is unusual. The Maritime Executive, a publication specialising in commercial shipping, said it was the first reported attack on a tanker in the western half of the Gulf in weeks.

Qatar has not commented on the reported attack, which falls within its exclusive economic zone.

Vessels have more commonly been targeted in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway linking the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.

Before the United States-Israel war on Iran began on February 28, the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day, and shipments through it accounted for about 20 percent of global crude and liquefied natural gas supplies.

In retaliation for US-Israeli attacks, Iran effectively closed the strait, while Washington has maintained a blockade on Iranian ports.

UKMTO said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.

Despite the attacks, oil exports from the Middle East have risen to, and according to provisional data even surpassed, pre-war levels in recent weeks.

The seven-day moving average of Middle East crude exports reached 18.3 million barrels per day (bpd) on September 30, compared with about 18 million bpd on average in the 12 months before the war, according to Kpler, a data firm.

entries.title: Democrats sue US President Trump over taxpayer-funded ad campaign
entries.summary: Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda.
entries.content:
Trump has faced a bipartisan backlash over ads that critics say violate prohibitions on taxpayer-funded propaganda.

The Democratic National Committee has filed a lawsuit against United States President Donald Trump over television advertisements that were publicly funded and allegedly used to promote his political policies.

Ken Martin, who heads the Democratic Party’s leadership body, suggested in a statement on Wednesday that the ads were designed to bolster Republican odds in the upcoming November 3 midterm elections.

“Donald Trump is misusing millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pure propaganda ads in a last-ditch attempt to save Republicans in November,” Martin said.

Later that day, Common Cause, a democracy watchdog group, filed a second lawsuit over the same set of ads.

It argued that the ads were “overtly political” and therefore ran afoul of laws that bar public funds from being used for political propaganda.

“These ads are not public-service announcements,” Common Cause said in its lawsuit, citing a justification Trump has offered for the television spots. “They are personal publicity and political propaganda through and through.”

Both lawsuits argue that, to create the ad campaign, Trump directed the White House to repurpose $20m in funds that Congress allocated for commemorative activities related to border security, including for those killed in the line of duty.

That manoeuvre, they argue, violates the separation of powers established in the US Constitution.

“The founders made clear more than 200 years ago that the executive can spend money only according to Congress’s direction,” Common Cause’s lawsuit said.

The two lawsuits also point to a provision Congress includes in its appropriations bills barring the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda purposes”.

Both complaints seek to have the ads declared illegal, and the expenditures stopped. They also call for steps to be taken to recover any money already spent on the ads.

The Democrats’ lawsuit was filed in Washington, DC, while the Common Cause complaint will be heard in the Southern District of New York.

Trump has faced mounting criticism over the ads, which began airing in September.

So far, the advertising campaign has cost more than $12m to run, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact.

The $20m Trump tapped for the ads comes from a $175m package Congress assigned to the Department of Homeland Security as part of Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda.

Critics have pointed out that one of the ads appears nearly identical to a television spot Trump used in his 2024 re-election campaign.

Three ads have aired so far. In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”.

The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.

On Wednesday, the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos released a poll showing the ads are highly unpopular. Some 86 percent of the Americans surveyed, including four out of five Republicans, said it was inappropriate for Trump to have used public money for them.

Trump has defended the ads as “promotion for the country”, and he has argued they were similar to public outreach campaigns put out by previous administrations.

But after a bipartisan backlash, Trump said on Monday that taxpayer funds would no longer be used for future ads.

He did not, however, commit to paying back the money already spent on the existing ads.

Members of Trump’s Republican Party have been among those speaking out against the ad campaign.

Senator Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, said the advertisements resembled something former Hungarian leader Viktor Orban would put out.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, meanwhile, indicated he agreed with the message in one of the advertisements, but he emphasised that “it shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars”.

entries.title: Yemeni government forces claim 1,860 Houthis ‘neutralised’
entries.summary: Yemeni government forces said in a social media post that they carried out 2,103 'precise targeting operations'.
entries.content:
Yemeni government forces said in a social media post that they carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations.”

Yemeni government forces said they have “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counter-offensive to retake territory under control of the rebel group.

The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s army said in a social media post early on Thursday local time that they carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” operation.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the “Dawn of Yemen” operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.

Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to capture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had captured in September.

Coalition targeting

The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.

The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement the targets included ballistic missile sites including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”.

The new operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport, according to the spokesperson.

Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said the attacks on the two airports killed three people.

One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.

entries.title: How kidnappings are hitting Nigeria’s Borno families hard
entries.summary: Across Borno, abductions are leaving families with depleted savings, missing loved ones and disrupted education.
entries.content:
Across Borno, abductions are leaving families with depleted savings, missing loved ones and disrupted education.

Maiduguri, Nigeria – When Musa Abdullahi Wakawa learned that his wife and seven-year-old son had been abducted, disbelief quickly gave way to fear.

Then came the question confronting many families caught in Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis: How could he raise the ransom demanded for their release?

For days, Musa searched for a way to bring his family home, confronting the financial burden imposed by the kidnappers.

Across northeastern Nigeria, families sell livestock, seek loans, dispose of property and exhaust savings in the hope of securing the release of loved ones.

In Borno State, kidnapping has become more than a security threat. Families are losing money, living with the trauma of abduction and, in some communities, keeping their children away from school.

‘Please just help me with your prayers’

Laraba Dauda, 45, still remembers the last conversation she had with her younger sister.

Her sister was abducted on January 13, 2026, along the Biu–Buratai road, according to Laraba.

Shortly after the abduction, the phone rang. Her sister was calling from somewhere in the bush.

“Aunty, unknown people have kidnapped us and taken us somewhere in the bush. We don’t know where they are taking us. At this moment, Aunty, please just help me with your prayers,” Laraba recalled her sister saying.

The call ended in tears.

Her sister has not returned home.

Months later, Laraba and her family still do not know where she is being held or whether she is safe.

Laraba is calling on the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to rescue those still in captivity.

“We need the government to come to our aid and help rescue our relatives who have spent more than six months in captivity,” she said.

A journey that never reached Maiduguri

For Anjikwi Hena, his son’s disappearance came just as the family was looking towards a better future.

His son was abducted on March 30, 2026, according to Hena.

He had completed his education and was preparing to travel to Maiduguri in search of work. His father encouraged him and prayed for his success.

Instead, the young man disappeared into captivity.

Hena said their close relationship has made the uncertainty especially painful.

When schools become unsafe

The kidnapping crisis is also threatening education in communities already weakened by years of rebellion.

In Askira-Uba Local Government Area of Borno State, only 56 of 113 primary schools are currently functioning, according to Fasuma Askira, the local government education secretary.

Before the May attack in Mussa, 76 primary schools were operating. The threat of violence subsequently forced authorities to close another 20, leaving only 56 functioning.

On May 15, suspected rebel fighters attacked Mussa and abducted dozens of children. A register later obtained by news services identified 40 missing children, although figures provided by the community and government have varied.

The Borno State government has more recently referred to about 44 children still missing from Mussa.

Then, on June 29, armed rebels attacked the Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking National Examinations Council examinations.

Some students were recovered shortly after the attack, but 36 students and a teacher have been reported as remaining in captivity.

The attacks have deepened fears among parents and teachers already living with the threat of rebel violence.

The education authority moved junior secondary students from Mussa to a government boarding school in Uba and advised the local government to deploy community vigilantes around schools.

Soldiers have also been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes, according to the Askira.

For families in these communities, keeping children in school now means weighing access to education against the risk of further attacks.

Borno’s crisis reflects a national problem

The situation in Borno is part of a wider kidnapping crisis across Nigeria.

Amnesty International Nigeria says at least 1,100 people were abducted across the country between January and April 2026, while warning that the actual figure could be considerably higher because many incidents in remote communities go unreported.

“Apart from killing people, gunmen are now on a rampage of abductions, largely for lucrative ransom,” said Isa Sanusi, director of Amnesty International Nigeria.

“Some stay months at the mercy of gunmen in punishing situations.”

Amnesty says victims can face torture, starvation and sexual violence, while families are often forced to raise money under extreme pressure.

The organisation has also warned that fear of abduction is pushing children out of school, particularly in rural communities.

Government says security and humanitarian measures are under way

Borno State Commissioner for Information and Internal Security Usman Tar said the government was using both military and nonmilitary measures to confront insecurity.

He acknowledged that the state has several security hotspots, including the Biu-Buratai axis and the Biu-Damboa-Sabon Gari area.

“We are putting in place both kinetic and non-kinetic measures in order to overcome the problem,” Tar said.

He said the state government was working closely with the armed forces by providing additional logistical support and civilian volunteers to assist field operations.

“This has enabled us to dominate the hotspot axis,” he said, adding that attacks had reduced in some affected areas.

The government is also using technology as part of its response, including drones equipped with thermal capabilities to monitor the movement of criminals, Tar said.

Authorities, he added, were advising commuters to avoid dangerous routes where necessary, and working to ensure that people involved in kidnapping and other criminal activities were prosecuted.

Tar acknowledged the humanitarian and psychological impact on families.

He said senior government officials had visited affected families to offer condolences and reassurance, while authorities also provided financial assistance through the State Emergency Management Agency and the state humanitarian agency.

“There are fixed sums that are provided through the State Emergency Management Agency and the State Humanitarian Agency,” Tar said, adding that other legitimate mechanisms were also used to make funding available to affected families.

He said the government viewed “terrorism and criminality” as problems that required more than military action.

“Terrorism is a multinational problem,” he said.

He pointed to poverty, unemployment and illiteracy as socioeconomic factors that can contribute to insecurity, saying federal and state governments were working to improve people’s access to necessities while ensuring that criminals face the law.

When kidnapping becomes a business

Security analyst Professor Khalifa Dikwa described the kidnapping situation as “pathetic”, warning that there were no clear signs that the crisis would end soon.

He said kidnapping for ransom had “metamorphosed into a profit-making venture”, with different armed groups competing for territory and, at times, fighting for dominance in forest areas.

According to Dikwa, ransom payments help sustain criminal networks, finance weapons purchases and attract younger recruits.

That creates a cycle in which communities already struggling with poverty are forced to finance the groups terrorising them.

Families may sell possessions to secure one relative’s release, only to face another ransom demand when someone else is abducted.

Dikwa argued that the government needs stronger intelligence- and technology-driven operations to locate armed groups and disrupt the movement of ransom money.

He also called for security agencies to receive modern weapons, night-vision equipment and tracking technology, alongside improved welfare for soldiers and other security personnel operating on the front lines.

For families, paying ransom may be the only immediate way to try to save someone they love. For armed groups, successful ransom payments can provide the resources and incentive to carry out further abductions.

The cost of waiting

Musa is waiting for his wife and young son. Laraba is waiting for her sister. Hena is waiting for the son who was preparing to leave home in search of work.

In Askira-Uba, 20 primary schools have closed since the Mussa attack, while dozens of children remain unaccounted for.

During their final phone call, Laraba’s sister told her:

“This is my last communication.”

entries.title: US stocks slide as oil prices fluctuate over renewed Iran war fears
entries.summary: Oil prices rose on fresh concerns about Middle East supplies, before falling on the possible release of more reserves.
entries.content:
Oil prices rose on fresh concerns about Middle East supplies, before falling over possible release of more reserves.

US financial markets have been whipsawed as bond market fears grow, pushing Treasury yields to their highest levels in more than 20 years, and oil prices continue to fluctuate, despite the Nasdaq and S&P 500 hitting record peaks.

Wall Street closed lower on Wednesday as oil prices rose then fell due to renewed concerns about disruption to Middle East supplies.

Stocks fell after closing at record highs in the previous session on Tuesday, with yields on US government bonds climbing to 24-year highs as investors worried about the impact of high oil prices on inflation and interest rates.

Oil prices increased on Thursday on persistent worries about supply from the Middle East amid an ⁠increase in attacks on ⁠shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.

‌Brent crude futures rose to $101.53 a barrel as of 01:16 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures climbed ⁠to $89.39 a barrel.

IEA member countries said they stand ready to release additional oil from their reserves if necessary and will prioritise diesel due to tight supplies of the fuel, the head of the organisation said on Wednesday.

G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed last Friday to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the United States-Iran war.

The latest announcement from the IEA calmed oil markets after prices had climbed on Wednesday following a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations.

The maritime agency said on Tuesday that there had been nine attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz this month, representing half of the September total in the waterway and the Gulf combined.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, repeated Washington’s claims that it was in control of the strait and that oil flows were at close to normal levels.

Gulf oil flows recover

Oil exports from the Gulf have recovered significantly in recent days, despite a surge in attacks on ships around the Strait of Hormuz, maritime experts and trackers say.

Gulf oil flows, excluding Iran, recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, while crude exports from the wider Middle East exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days during the month, maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported.

However, the recovery has come as attacks on tankers increase and shipping companies face higher freight, insurance and security costs.

On Tuesday, 12 crew members on a Panama-flagged tanker were injured in an attack by an unknown projectile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement.
